title: Empiricism, calibration and velocity
blurb: Explain why agile plans are built from evidence, what calibration and velocity mean, and how plans are refreshed every iteration.
question: A new delivery team is asked to forecast when its first release will be ready. Which planning approach does PRINCE2 Agile favour, and what evidence should the forecast use?

teach.h: Plan from what is actually happening
teach.body: Most agile methods rest on empiricism: making decisions from experience, meaning what is happening now or has already happened. In plain English, you start the work, watch how much really gets done, and use that rate to forecast the end date. The plans practice in PRINCE2 Agile builds on this idea rather than trying to predict everything before work starts.

Starting work and seeing how much gets done is sometimes called calibration, like setting weighing scales to zero before you weigh anything, or calculating velocity, meaning the rate of progress. Velocity is the average number of story points a team delivers per timebox. It is a team's own measure: forecasting with another team's or one person's rate breaks the empirical approach.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3, 12.4.3 and Glossary

teach.caption: (14 + 19 + 18) / 3 = 17 points per iteration. With 85 points left, the team forecasts five more iterations.

teach.h: Replan every iteration, just in time
teach.body: Because forecasts come from real progress, plans are refreshed often. Each iteration starts with a team planning workshop, where the team estimates stories and selects what it can realistically deliver. During the stage the project manager updates the release map with actuals, forecasts and adjustments. Detailed task planning is done only for the next iteration, so effort is not wasted planning too far ahead.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3, 8.3.2.5; Tables 13.9 and 13.13

head: When
What is updated
Where
rows: Team plan for the next iteration
Release map for the next stage

teach.body: Calderbrook is building a repairs-reporting app for tenants. After three iterations, team coach Femi Adebayo shows the team delivered 14, 19 and 18 points, so its velocity is 17. Project manager Claire Holt has 85 points left in the release and forecasts five more iterations. A director suggests using the faster rate of a sister team. Claire declines: the forecast must come from this team's own measured progress.

teach.text: Empiricism is the agile preference; rationalism (predicting by logic before work starts) is its opposite. Calibration does not mean checking quality or borrowing a benchmark: it means starting real work and measuring it. A team forecasts from its own measured velocity and refreshes the forecast as conditions change.

items: Empiricism: decide from what is happening or has happened (8.3).
Rationalism, planning by reasoning and logic, is the opposite.
Calibration or calculating velocity: start work and measure the rate.
Velocity = average story points delivered per timebox, for your own team.
Forecast: points remaining divided by velocity.
Replan each iteration; detailed task plans cover the next iteration.

summary: You can now explain empiricism and its opposite, rationalism, and describe calibration and velocity as the evidence agile plans rest on. You can also show where plans are refreshed: each iteration, during the stage and at stage boundaries.

A.q: What is empiricism in PRINCE2 Agile planning?
options: Detailed task plans made for the whole project before it starts
Making decisions based on what is happening or has happened
Fixing estimates at initiation so the board can approve them
Using the project manager's logic to predict the end date
A.why: Empiricism means deciding from experience: start work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that (book 8.3).

whyNot.0: Planning every task up front is prediction, not learning from experience; agile plans detail only the next iteration.
whyNot.2: Fixing estimates before work starts is a predictive approach, not an empirical one.
whyNot.3: Predicting by reasoning and logic is rationalism, the opposite of empiricism.

A.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile call the opposite of empiricism?
A.why: Rationalism, where reasoning or logic is used to predict and plan what should happen, is the opposite of empiricism (8.3).

whyNot.0: Calibration is part of empiricism: starting work and measuring how much gets done.
whyNot.1: Timeboxing fixes the length of a period of work; it is not the opposite of empiricism.
whyNot.2: Velocity is the measured rate of progress that empiricism relies on.

options: The average story points a team delivers per timebox
The number of user stories left in the product backlog
The hours each developer is available per iteration
The time one user story takes from start to done
A.why: Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox, used to forecast if conditions stay the same (12.4.3, Glossary).

whyNot.1: Stories remaining are the work still to do, not a rate of delivery.
whyNot.2: Available hours describe capacity in time, not points delivered.
whyNot.3: The elapsed time for one item is closer to cycle time than to velocity.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Starting work and seeing how much is getting done is sometimes called [?], in a similar way to setting weighing scales to zero.
B.why: The book likens starting work and measuring progress to zeroing scales and calls it calibration, or calculating velocity (8.3).

whyNot.0: Baselining fixes an approved version of a product for change control; it is not about measuring the rate of work.
whyNot.1: Timeboxing sets a fixed period for work; it does not measure how much gets done.
whyNot.3: Refactoring improves a product's internal structure without changing its behaviour.

B.q: A team delivered 21, 17 and 19 story points in its last three iterations. The release has 95 points remaining. How many more iterations should it forecast?

whyNot.0: Four iterations would need a velocity of about 24, well above what the team has achieved.
whyNot.2: Six iterations assumes about 16 points per iteration, below the team's average of 19.
whyNot.3: Seven iterations assumes under 14 points per iteration, lower than any recent result.

B.q:
Which two statements about planning in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Empiricism forecasts from what is actually happening.
2. A new team should forecast with a sister team's velocity.
3. Starting work and measuring progress is sometimes called calculating velocity.
4. Rationalism is the approach most agile methods are based on.
B.why: Statements 1 and 3 match book 8.3: empiricism uses experience, and starting work to see the rate is called calibration or calculating velocity.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: a team should use its own velocity, not another team's.
whyNot.2: Both are false: use your own team's velocity, and most agile methods rest on empiricism.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: rationalism is the opposite of the empiricism agile methods rely on.

C.q: A team has finished two iterations of a new project. Which evidence should it use to forecast, and what is this called?
options: A sister team's measured rate; calibration
Its own measured rate; rationalist planning
Its own measured rate; calculating velocity
C.why: The team uses its own measured progress, which the book calls calibration or calculating velocity (8.3).

whyNot.0: Another team's rate is not this team's evidence, so it is not calibration.
whyNot.1: A logical estimate is rationalism, not empiricism.
whyNot.2: The evidence is right but the name is wrong: rationalism means planning by reasoning and logic.

C.q: When is the detailed plan for the next iteration produced, and in which workshop?
options: Each iteration, in the team planning workshop
Each stage boundary, in the release planning workshop
Once in initiation, in the project initiation workshop
Each iteration, in the progress review workshop
C.why: The team planning workshop prepares for the next iteration; its iteration planning topic produces a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

whyNot.1: The release planning workshop updates the high-level release map for the next stage, not the task-level plan.
whyNot.2: The project initiation workshop develops a high-level release map, not iteration task plans.
whyNot.3: The progress review workshop reviews project status and demos; it does not plan the next iteration.

C.q: After iteration 4, two experienced developers leave and the team's delivery rate drops. What should happen to the release map forecast?
options: Stay as baselined until the stage boundary
Use the rate from the team's first iteration
Be updated from the latest measured progress
Be reset to the estimate made at initiation
C.why: Velocity forecasts hold only while conditions stay the same, and the PM updates the release map with actuals and forecasts during the stage (8.3, Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Waiting until the boundary hides a known change; the release map is updated with forecasts during the stage.
whyNot.1: An early rate reflects a team that no longer exists in that form.
whyNot.3: Returning to an initiation estimate swaps evidence for prediction, which is rationalism.

reteach.title: Learn your speed by driving
reteach.question: On a new commute, would you trust a guess about the journey time, or your timing from the first few trips?

blocks.body: Agile teams treat a plan like a new commute. Instead of reasoning out the answer in advance, they start the work, time it, and forecast from what they saw. That is empiricism. The first iterations calibrate the team, and the average rate they reveal is the velocity.

blocks.h: From real work to a forecast

blocks.text: A forecast from someone else's speed, or from logic alone, is not empirical. Use the team's own measured rate and refresh it as things change.

explain.body: Empiricism decides from experience of what is happening or has happened. Rationalism predicts by reasoning and logic before work starts. Agile methods favour empiricism.

test.q: Planning by reasoning and logic to predict what should happen is called:
test.why: Rationalism uses reasoning or logic to predict and plan; it is the opposite of empiricism (8.3).

whyNot.0: Empiricism relies on experience, not prediction by logic.
whyNot.1: Calibration is starting work and measuring the rate of progress.
whyNot.3: Velocity is the measured rate of story points delivered per timebox.

explain.body: Like zeroing scales before weighing, calibration means starting real work and seeing how much gets done, giving a true reference for forecasting.

test.q: A team with no history begins its first iteration. What does calibration involve?
options: Doing real work and measuring how much gets done
Agreeing story point values with a sister team
Setting the board's time tolerance to zero
Converting every story estimate into hours
test.why: Calibration is starting work and seeing how much is getting done (8.3).

whyNot.1: Borrowing another team's reference is not measuring this team's work.
whyNot.2: Zero time tolerance is a fix-and-flex default, not calibration.
whyNot.3: Converting points to hours abandons relative estimation and measures nothing.

explain.body: Velocity is the average story points a team delivers per timebox. Divide the points remaining by it to forecast how many iterations are left.

test.q: A team delivered 12, 16 and 14 points in three iterations. What is its velocity?

whyNot.0: 12 is the lowest single result, not the average.
whyNot.2: 16 is the highest single result, not the average.
whyNot.3: 42 is the total over three iterations, not the rate per iteration.

explain.body: The release map stays high level and is updated with actuals and forecasts. Task-level plans are made for the next iteration only, in managing product delivery.

test.q: In which process does task-level planning for the next iteration take place?
test.why: The team plans the next iteration at task level in managing product delivery, in the team planning workshop (8.3.2.5, Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: The stage boundary updates the high-level release map, not task plans.
whyNot.1: Initiation documents a high-level release map for the project.
whyNot.2: Directing a project is where the board makes key decisions; it does not plan tasks.
